e.etymology: A short form of the Yoruba name Folasade, honor confers a crown. Americans took it up in the 1980s after the Nigerian-born British singer Sade. An unrelated Finnish Sade means rain.

assoc.t: Marquis de Sade, source of the word sadism

e.note: Often misread as rhyming with fade; it is said shah-DAY.

e.etymology: A spelling of Alana, the feminine form of Alan, a Breton name of uncertain meaning that the Normans brought to Britain. Alannah is also linked to the Irish endearment a leanbh, child.
A Yoruba oriki, or praise name, built from ja, to fight, and ni, to have: a child his parents struggled to have.

assoc.t: Ajani Goldmane, lion hero in Magic: The Gathering

e.etymology: From Greek Nestor, probably related to neomai, to return safely, and nostos, homecoming. In Homer, Nestor is the aged king of Pylos whose advice the Greeks rely on at Troy.
namesakes: Nestor (wise old king in Homer's Iliad)

e.etymology: A modern American name in the pattern of Jabari, Jamari and Jakari. It is sometimes connected with Johari, the Swahili word for jewel.
The Urdu, Persian and Hausa form of Arabic Uthman, the name of the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, a companion of the Prophet Muhammad. The Turkish form is Osman.
From short forms of old Germanic names built on wolf, such as Wolfgang and Wolfram, and from the English word itself. In Yiddish tradition Wolf is paired with the Hebrew name Ze'ev.
A form of Rosalind, an old Germanic name from hros, horse, and lind, gentle or serpent. Since the Middle Ages it has been read as Latin rosa linda, and in Spanish it means pretty rose.
A spelling of Giovanni, the Italian form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. The Geo- spelling is used mostly by Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking families.
An older spelling of Ivy, the evergreen climbing plant, from Old English ifig. It was given in the late 1800s and is also an English surname.
A double-n spelling of Luciana, the feminine of the Roman name Lucianus, derived from Lucius and Latin lux, light. Many also read it as Lucy plus Anna.

e.meaning: mythical bird reborn from its ashes
e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Phoenix, from Greek phoinix, the mythical bird that burns and rises again from its ashes. It is also close to fénix, the Spanish spelling of the word.

assoc.t: Marcus Fenix, hero of the Gears of War games

e.etymology: The English word, from Old English herebeorg, shelter or lodging. As a name it joins River, Ocean and Haven; Harbour is also an English surname.
In American use a modern name, a spelling of Anaya that also echoes Amaya and Naia. Anaiah is a minor Old Testament name, Hebrew for the Lord has answered.

e.meaning: of Idalion, a title of the goddess Aphrodite
e.etymology: From Idalia, a title of Aphrodite taken from Idalion, a city in Cyprus where she was worshipped. The name is used in Spanish, Polish and Italian.

assoc.t: Hurricane Idalia, which struck Florida in August 2023

e.etymology: A spelling of Gianni, the Italian short form of Giovanni (John), from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. The o brings it closer to the nickname Gio.
A pet form of Philippa, the feminine of Philip, from Greek philos, loving, and hippos, horse. Robert Browning's 1841 verse drama Pippa Passes spread it, and it remains chiefly British.
namesakes: Pippa Middleton (sister of Catherine, Princess of Wales)
e.note: Pippa is crude slang in Italian and Swedish; worth knowing for families with ties there.

assoc.t: Pippa Middleton, sister of the Princess of Wales

e.etymology: Sanskrit nirvana, literally a blowing out, as of a flame: in Buddhism the release from desire, suffering and rebirth. In English it also means a state of perfect bliss.
An English surname from Lar-kin, a medieval pet form of Laurence, and an Irish one from O Lorcain, descendant of Lorcan, fierce. Today it also reads as a longer form of Lark.
The Spanish and Portuguese form of Gershom, the son of Moses, whose name the book of Exodus explains as a stranger there. It is well used in Latin America.
A modern name, a short form of Alayna and Elaina and a relative of Laney. Elaine and its kin come from the Old French form of Helen.
A modern elaboration of Ellie with the French -ette ending. France has a similar name, Eliette, a feminine pet form of Elie (Elijah).
From the English city and surname, Old English ceaster, a Roman fort or walled town, from Latin castra, camp.
namesakes: Chester Bennington (lead singer of Linkin Park)

assoc.t: Chester, walled cathedral city in England

e.note: Rhymes with molester; Chester the Molester is a long-running playground taunt.

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Josephine, a feminine of Joseph, from Hebrew Yosef, he will add. Fina, Pepa and Pepita are its traditional Spanish pet forms.
namesakes: Josefina Montoya (American Girl doll from 1820s New Mexico)

e.etymology: A French-styled form of Arabella, a medieval Scottish name that probably began as a variant of Annabel. It has long been linked with Latin orabilis, yielding to prayer.
A spelling of Kason, a modern American name that rhymes with Jason and Mason and echoes the English surname Cason.
From Greek Eunike, good victory, from eu, good, and nike, victory. In the New Testament Eunice is the mother of Timothy, praised for her sincere faith.
namesakes: Eunice Kennedy Shriver (founder of the Special Olympics)

e.etymology: A spelling of Aislinn, from Irish aisling, dream or vision, also the name of a kind of Irish poem in which Ireland appears as a woman in a dream. In Ireland it is said ASH-ling.
From the Dutch surname prefix van der, of the or from the, as in Vanderbilt. Vander is also a first name in Brazil, and a character of that name appears in the animated series Arcane.

assoc.t: Vander, the father figure in Netflix's Arcane

e.etymology: An English place name and surname from Old English read, red, and leah, a woodland clearing.
namesakes: Boo Radley (the reclusive neighbor in To Kill a Mockingbird)

assoc.t: Boo Radley of To Kill a Mockingbird

e.etymology: A dressed-up spelling of Royal, from Old French roial and Latin regalis, of a king. Royale is the French feminine form, familiar in English from Casino Royale and battle royale.

assoc.t: Casino Royale, the James Bond novel and film
battle royale, a last-one-standing fight or game mode

e.meaning: row of houses by a wood
e.etymology: An English surname for someone who lived in a row of cottages by a wood. Americans took it up as a first name in the 1910s in honor of President Woodrow Wilson.
namesakes: Woody Guthrie (folk singer, born Woodrow Wilson Guthrie)
